quote: Let us see, then, in what order the high priest is appointed. "Moses," he says, "gathered together the congregation, and says to them: This is the word which the Lord commanded." Although, therefore, the Lord had commanded concerning the appointing of the high priest and the Lord had chosen him, nevertheless the congregation too is gathered together. For in the ordination of a priest there is required also the presence of the people, so that all may know and be assured that the one who is more excellent out of all the people, who is more learned, who is more holy, who is more eminent in every virtue, that one is chosen for the priesthood, and this with the people standing by, lest afterward any reconsideration should arise for anyone, lest any scruple should remain. This is, moreover, what the Apostle too commanded in the ordination of a priest, saying: "It is fitting also that he have…

Well is the church named ecclesia ["assembly"], because it calls forth and assembles all men, as the Lord says in Leviticus: "Then assemble the whole community at the entrance of the meeting tent." It is worthy of note that this word assemble is used in the Scriptures for the first time in the passage when the Lord established Aaron in the high priesthood. In Deuteronomy God says to Moses, "Assemble the people for me; I will have them hear my words, that they may learn to fear me." He mentions the name of the church again when he says of the tablets: "And on them were inscribed all the words that the Lord spoke to you on the mountain from the midst of the fire on the day of the assembly"; as if he would say more plainly, "on the day on which you were called and gathered together." And the psalmist says, "I will give you thanks in a great church [ecclesia], in the mighty throng I will…

With attentive ears and watchful heart hear the consecration of the high priest, or of the priest, because you too, according to the promises of God, are priests of the Lord: "for you are a holy nation and a priesthood." Moses, he says, took according to the command of the Lord "Aaron and his sons", and first indeed he washes them, and afterward he clothes them. Consider more carefully the order of the words: first he washes, afterward he clothes. For you cannot be clothed unless you have first been washed. "Wash yourselves," therefore, "and be clean, and take away your wickednesses from your souls." For unless you have been washed in this manner, you cannot put on the Lord Jesus Christ, according to what the Apostle says: "Put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh in its lusts." Let Moses, therefore, wash you, let him himself wash you and let him himself clothe…

So then he washed him and clothed him. With what garment? "With a tunic," he says, "and he girded him with the girdle, and again he clothed him with the ankle-length tunic", or, as we read elsewhere, "the inner tunic". With two tunics, as I see, the high priest is clothed through Moses. But what do we make of the fact that Jesus forbade his priests, our Apostles, to use two tunics? And we had said that Moses and Jesus, that is, the law and the gospels, are consonant with one another. Someone might perhaps be able to say that what Jesus commanded, that two tunics are not to be had, is not contrary to the law, but more perfect than the law, just as when the law forbids murder, but Jesus cuts away even anger, and when the law prohibits adultery, Jesus cuts off even the concupiscence of the heart. So then it will seem that there the high priest was clothed with two tunics, and here the…

"And he girded him," he says, "according to the making of the ephod." Already above too he had said that "he girded him with the girdle" over the tunic, and now again he is girded "according to the making of the ephod". What is this double girdle, with which he wishes the high priest to be bound fast on every side? Let him be bound fast in word, bound fast in work, ready for all things, nothing slack, let him have nothing loose. Let him be girded with the virtues of the soul, let him be bound fast from bodily vices, let him fear no lapse of the soul, none of the body, let him always use both girdles, "that he may be chaste in body and spirit". And well is it that he is girded also "according to the making of the ephod". For according to his own deeds and according to his own works he will use the girdle of virtue. And after these things, he says, "he put upon him the breastpiece"—which…

But he has not yet finished, and yet another ornament is to be added; it is necessary that he receive also a crown. Therefore he receives first the "cidaris", which is either a certain covering of the head or an ornament. And after these things there is set upon him the "mitre". "Before the face", that is, from the forehead of the high priest, "the golden plate, hallowed", on which the name of God is said to be engraved. Truly this ornament of the head, where the name of God is said to be placed, is set on above all those things with which the lower members of the body had been adorned. In this it seems to me to be indicated that above all things which can be perceived or understood, whether of the world or of the rest of creatures, the knowledge of God is more eminent, as of the author of all things. And because he himself "is the head of all things", therefore this ornament too is set…

You must know that this chrism [chrismation] is prefigured in the Old Testament. When Moses, conferring on his brother the divine appointment, was ordering him high priest, he anointed him after he had bathed in water, and thenceforward he was called "christ" ["anointed"], clearly after the figurative Chrism.

But as for what he says: "And Moses brought near the sons of Aaron, and clothed them with tunics and girded them with girdles and put upon them cidaras, as the Lord commanded Moses", it must be attended to what is the difference of the lesser priests to the greater priesthoods. To these neither are double vestments handed over, nor the "ephod", nor the "rational", nor the "ornament of the head", but only the "cidaris" and the "girdles", which bind the tunic. These too, then, receive the grace of the priesthood, and these too discharge the office, but not as that one who is adorned both with the "ephod" and the "rational", who is resplendent "with manifestation and truth", who is decorated with the ornament of the "golden plate". Whence I judge it to be one thing among priests to discharge the office, and another to be instructed in all things and adorned. For anyone can discharge the…
